section.title: Restore Us, O God
section.sectionRationale: An Asaphite lament for the Northern Kingdom, likely prayed as Assyrian threat pressed on Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. A rising threefold refrain, 'restore us,' frames a shift from shepherd to vine imagery, climaxing in a plea for 'the son of man' at God's right hand.
section.thesis: When God's own vine lies broken down and ravaged, His people's only hope is not their own strength but God's face shining again, embodied at last in the Son of Man at His right hand, upon whom restoration finally rests.
section.frameNote: Four movements, each intensifying the divine title in the refrain: the cry to the Shepherd of Israel, 1-3; lament over God's anger, 4-7; the vine from Egypt now ravaged, 8-13; and the plea for the son of man at God's right hand, 14-19.

units.label: Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel
units.note: the cry to the enthroned Shepherd

verses.text: Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock; You who sit enthroned between the cherubim, shine forth
before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Rally Your mighty power and come to save us.
{{shuv|Restore}} us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.

units.label: How long will Your anger smolder

verses.text: O LORD God of Hosts, how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people?
You fed them with the bread of tears and made them drink the full measure of their tears.
You make us contend with our neighbors; our enemies mock us.
Restore us, O God of Hosts, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.

units.label: The vine from Egypt, now ravaged

verses.text: You uprooted a {{gefen|vine}} from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it.
You cleared the ground for it, and it took root and filled the land.
The mountains were covered by its shade, and the mighty cedars with its branches.
It sent out its branches to the Sea, and its shoots toward the River.
Why have You broken down its walls, so that all who pass by pick its fruit?
The boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed upon it.

units.label: The son of man at Your right hand
units.note: the final, personal plea for restoration

verses.text: Return, O God of Hosts, we pray! Look down from heaven and see! Attend to this vine,
the root Your right hand has planted, the son You have raised up for Yourself.
Your vine has been cut down and burned; they perish at the rebuke of Your countenance.
Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand, on the {{benadam|son of man}} You have raised up for Yourself.
Then we will not turn away from You; revive us, and we will call on Your name.
Restore us, O LORD God of Hosts; cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.

shuv.gloss: To turn back, return, or restore. The refrain 'restore us' asks God to turn His people back to Himself and turn His own face back toward them, growing in intensity with each repetition, verses 3, 7, 19.

gefen.gloss: A vine or grapevine. Israel is pictured as a vine God Himself transplanted from Egypt and once caused to flourish over the whole land, an image Jesus later takes up directly of Himself, John 15:1.

benadam.gloss: Son of man, literally a human being. Here it names the man at God's right hand on whom restoration depends, language later charged with messianic meaning in Daniel 7:13 and taken by Jesus as His own title.

basic.context: Written for the northern tribes, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh, this psalm pictures God as Shepherd, then as the One who planted Israel like a vine out of Egypt. Now the vine is broken down, ravaged by wild boars, and the psalm's threefold refrain grows more urgent, restore us, cause Your face to shine, until it lands on a plea for the son of man at God's right hand.
basic.hermeneutics: The lament is real and historical, most likely from a period of northern crisis before Assyria's conquest, yet its climactic language, 'the man at Your right hand,' 'the son of man,' outgrows any single king and opens toward a fuller, messianic answer.
basic.originalLanguages: The refrain begs God to shuv, restore or turn back, His people and His own shining face. Israel is a gefen, vine, transplanted from Egypt, and the psalm's hope finally rests on ben adam, a son of man, at God's right hand, language Daniel 7:13 and the Gospels later take up directly of Christ.
basic.typology: The vine brought from Egypt and ravaged points forward to Jesus, the true vine, John 15:1, who succeeds where Israel failed. The 'son of man' raised up at God's right hand anticipates Christ, exalted to God's right hand as the Danielic Son of Man, Acts 5:31.
basic.christ: Jesus takes up the vine imagery of this psalm directly, calling Himself 'the true vine,' John 15:1, and He is the Son of Man exalted to God's right hand, the very position and title this psalm longs to see filled, Daniel 7:13, Acts 5:31.
basic.god: God is both Shepherd and Vinedresser, the one who planted and once made Israel flourish, and also the one whose anger, though real, is not the last word; His people can appeal to His own character to restore what He Himself once caused to grow.
basic.crossReferences: John 15:1-5 shows Jesus as the true vine, the deeper fulfillment of Israel's calling. Daniel 7:13 supplies the messianic weight later attached to 'son of man.' Numbers 6:24-26 stands behind the refrain's plea for God's face to shine, the priestly blessing this psalm turns into prayer.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's rising cry for restoration, from Shepherd to vine to the son of man at God's right hand, finds its answer in Jesus, the true vine and the exalted Son of Man, in whom God's face finally and permanently shines on His people.

context.literary:
Psalm 80 is held together by a refrain that is not quite a repeat. It appears at verses 3, 7 and 19, and each time the divine title grows: 'O God,' then 'O God of Hosts,' then 'O LORD God of Hosts.' Between the second and third occurrences the address 'God of Hosts' sounds again at verse 14, and 'LORD God of Hosts' opens verse 4. The people are climbing a ladder of names, and the last rung is the covenant name itself. The request is the same each time, that God restore them, let His face shine, and save them, but it is prayed with growing boldness.

The stanzas between the refrains use different pictures. Verses 1-2 address the Shepherd who leads Joseph like a flock and sits between the cherubim. Verses 4-6 name the pain: anger that smolders against the people's own prayers, bread of tears, and the neighbors' contempt. Verses 8-13 tell a long story of a vine, planted, spread to the sea and the river, and then left with its walls down. Verses 14-19 turn the story into a plea.

A mirror pattern sits inside the last stanza. Verse 15 speaks of the son whom God 'raised up for Yourself,' and verse 17 uses almost the same phrase for the 'son of man You have raised up for Yourself.' The vine and the man are set side by side, as if the people are pointing at one and asking for the other. The face of God also frames the psalm's tension: the refrain begs for the face to shine, and verse 16 says the vine is burned 'at the rebuke of Your countenance.' The same face can shine or rebuke, and the prayer asks God to choose the shining.
context.historical:
The psalm names Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, tribes descended from Rachel by way of Joseph and Benjamin, Genesis 35:16-18. In Israel's wilderness camp these three marched together behind the ark, Numbers 2:17-24, so an ear tuned to Israel's early story would hear them as the tribes that followed the ark. The address to the One who sits enthroned between the cherubim fits: that was the title of the LORD attached to the ark, 1 Samuel 4:4 and 2 Samuel 6:2. This has led some to date the psalm early, in the shadow of the ark's loss in the days of Shiloh.

Most readers place it in the last decades of the northern kingdom, when Assyria stripped away territory, 2 Kings 15:29, and finally took Samaria and carried Israel off, 2 Kings 17:5-6. The tribes named in verse 2 were the heart of that kingdom, and the Assyrian pressure suits the language of a vine trampled by all who pass by. A third possibility is that the psalm was prayed in Judah after 722 BC, for the northern survivors. The text gives no name of a king or an enemy, and that silence is probably deliberate, since it lets each generation of God's people pray it in a similar crisis.

The picture of a vine from Egypt planted in the land, its shade covering mountains and its branches reaching 'the Sea' and 'the River,' verses 10-11, recalls the ideal borders of the promised land, from the Mediterranean to the Euphrates, Exodus 23:31, and the reach of the king's rule in Psalm 72:8. The vine had, in memory, once stretched over the whole inheritance. The wild boar of verse 13 was an unclean animal to Israel, Leviticus 11:7, so its invasion adds the sense of defilement to the sense of loss.
context.canonical:
Psalm 80 draws on three older streams. The shepherd language goes back to Jacob, who blessed Joseph's sons by saying that God had been his shepherd all his life, Genesis 48:15, and who called God 'the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel,' Genesis 49:24, in the same blessing where Joseph is a fruitful vine, Genesis 49:22. The refrain reworks the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, 'may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you,' turning it from a benediction into a prayer for what the people no longer feel. And the vine belongs to a set of Old Testament images of Israel, such as Isaiah 5:1-7, Jeremiah 2:21, Hosea 10:1 and Ezekiel 19:10-14.

Within the Psalter, the psalm continues the run of Asaphite laments. Psalm 79 cries that the nations have devoured God's inheritance, Psalm 80 pleads for the ravaged vine, and Psalm 81 recalls what God said when Israel would not listen. The third refrain, with its full title, is echoed in later prayers such as Daniel 9:17, where the exile asks God to cause His face to shine on the desolate sanctuary.

In the New Testament the vine passes to Christ. Jesus tells of a vineyard whose tenants beat the servants and kill the landowner's son, Matthew 21:33-41, an echo of Isaiah 5 with a Son at its center, and then He says, 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1. The 'son of man' of verse 17 comes into focus alongside Daniel 7:13-14, Psalm 110:1 and Jesus' own use of the title in Mark 14:61-62.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was composed so that a people in trouble could pray with hope and without pretense. The author does not say the troubles are undeserved. He admits God is angry, verse 4, and he attributes the breach in the wall to God's hand, verse 12. That honesty is what makes the request believable: they are asking a God they know has acted against them to turn and act for them.

The author's method is to remind God, and the people, of who He has been. The image of the vine does that work. Israel is not a nation that grew on its own but one that God pulled up out of Egypt and planted, and whose growth was His doing. The argument is simple: what You planted, You cannot ignore.

The psalm also refuses to let the crisis be only political. Each refrain asks for God's face, not just for a change in circumstances. Restoration for these people means seeing the light of God's presence again, and the salvation they ask for, 'that we may be saved,' comes from that. The final lines promise a response, 'we will not turn away from You,' but the promise follows the request for revival, verse 18. Asaph makes clear who must act first. The people cannot turn themselves; they need to be turned, and they say so.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a moment of national disaster and a community's honest prayer. It does not prescribe a particular political response, and it does not promise that every prayer of this shape will be answered in the same visible way. What it gives is a pattern of prayer.

The pattern has movements that carry into any age. Begin with who God is, in this case Shepherd and Vinedresser. Say plainly what hurts, including the fear that God is angry at the prayers themselves. Recall what He has done. Then ask for the restoring of His face, and promise a life of calling on His name.

The vine language of verses 12 and 13 should not be lifted into a fixed doctrine about how or when God allows his people to be plundered. The psalm asks 'Why?' and does not fully answer. The New Testament is more direct, with its warning that branches can be cut off, John 15:6 and Romans 11:17-22, but the psalm itself is content to ask. The text also should not be turned into a demand that God repeat any previous rescue in any given place. It teaches instead that God's people may ask Him for restoration boldly, that they should do so on the ground of what He is, and that the answer they seek is finally His own face.

debates.question: Does 'the man at Your right hand... the son of man' in verse 17 refer to a reigning Davidic king of the psalmist's own day, or does it point forward messianically?

views.label: Primarily the reigning king or the nation itself, personified as the one through whom God's covenant favor would be restored
views.case: The immediate context concerns national deliverance for specific tribes under real threat, and 'son of man' can simply mean 'a human being,' fitting a contemporary royal figure, as in Psalm 8:4 where the phrase names mankind.

views.label: A deliberately open messianic title that later Scripture, especially Daniel 7:13 and the Gospels, fills with its fullest meaning in Christ
views.case: The language exceeds any single historical king's actual deliverance, and the New Testament applies 'Son of Man' and exaltation to God's right hand directly and repeatedly to Jesus, Mark 14:62 and Acts 7:56.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the psalm looks for a human figure at God's right hand through whom restoration comes, a hope Scripture shows fulfilled beyond any merely historical king in Jesus Christ.

debates.question: Who is the 'son' of verse 15, and how does he relate to the 'son of man' of verse 17?

views.label: The same figure: the king, or a coming deliverer, whom God has strengthened for Himself
views.case: The two verses use nearly the same words, that God 'raised up' a son 'for Yourself.' The repeated phrase suggests a single person, so that the vine's rescue depends on the one whom God has made strong.

views.label: Two related figures: Israel as God's son, then the king who represents Israel
views.case: Israel is called God's son in Exodus 4:22 and Hosea 11:1, so the first mention can name the people as the shoot God planted. Verse 17 then asks for a man to stand for them, in the way the Davidic king does in Psalm 2:6-7.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew of the first line of verse 15 is difficult and translations divide on it, so caution is wise. Either way, the psalm links the people's fate to a chosen son of God and prays that His hand be on him.

debates.question: When was the psalm written, and for whom?

views.label: Before 722 BC, for the northern tribes under Assyrian pressure
views.case: The naming of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh suits the northern kingdom, and the ravaged vine fits the loss of territory under Assyria, 2 Kings 15:29.

views.label: Early, in the time of the ark at Shiloh
views.case: The address to the One enthroned between the cherubim and the march order of Numbers 2 place these tribes behind the ark, and 1 Samuel 4:4 links the title to Shiloh.

views.label: After 722 BC, as a prayer in Judah for the scattered north
views.case: The Asaphite collection was kept and used in Judah, and the psalm's broken walls and burned vine can look back on completed ruin, as in 2 Kings 17:5-6.

debates.bearing: The psalm does not depend on an answer. In every proposed setting, God's people are asking the Shepherd of Israel to return, and the psalm was kept because later generations could pray it too.

study.originalLanguages:
The refrain asks God to 'cause Your face to shine,' from the Hebrew verb for making light, in the same form as the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25. A face that shines is a face turned toward someone in favor, and the same phrase becomes a prayer in Psalm 31:16, Psalm 67:1 and Daniel 9:17. The prayer for shining is set against verse 16, where the vine perishes 'at the rebuke of Your countenance.' The Hebrew for the face is the same word in both places, so the psalm asks that the face that rebukes be the face that shines.

Verse 1 calls on God to 'shine forth,' the verb Deuteronomy 33:2 uses of the LORD shining forth from Mount Paran, and Psalm 94:1 uses to call on the God of vengeance. It is the language of a theophany, of God appearing in glory to act. The next verse asks Him to 'rally' His mighty power, from a verb that means to rouse or stir up, a word for waking a sleeper. The people are asking God to show Himself and to move.

Verse 4 says God's anger 'smolders,' a verb built on smoke. The same verb appears in Psalm 74:1 of the anger against the sheep of His pasture. The unusual thing is the object: the anger smolders 'against the prayers of Your people.' The very act of praying has met with resistance, or seems to. It is the honest voice of people who feel God is not listening. Verse 5 adds 'the bread of tears,' a phrase kin to Psalm 42:3, where tears have been a person's food.

In verse 8, the vine is 'uprooted' out of Egypt. The verb is the one used for pulling up the pegs of a tent and setting out on a journey, so the vine is imagined as a wanderer, a camp on the move that God then plants. The verb for planting in that verse and again in verse 15 is the one behind Exodus 15:17, where God 'will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance.' The psalm remembers the Song of the Sea as a work of gardening.

In verse 10 the 'mighty cedars' are, literally, cedars of God, a Hebrew way of saying the greatest of trees. The vine did not just reach the mountains; it overshadowed the finest cedars. The word for the broken walls in verse 12 has a close echo in Isaiah 5:5 and Psalm 89:40, both of which speak of God tearing down walls. Verse 13 names the 'boar from the forest,' an unclean animal, and 'the creatures of the field.'

Finally, in verse 17 the man is 'at Your right hand.' The right hand in the psalm is God's planting hand in verse 15 and now His place of honor. Benjamin's name means son of the right hand, Genesis 35:18, and the tribe is named in verse 2, so the phrase may carry an echo of that name, though the text does not spell it out. In verse 18 the request is 'revive us,' a verb that means give life, followed by the promise to call on God's name.

typology.type: The vine planted and pruned, Psalm 80:8-16
typology.fulfillment: Israel is God's vine, brought out of Egypt and planted with care. Isaiah 5:1-7 says the vine yielded sour grapes, and Jeremiah 2:21 says it became wild. Jesus takes the image and reverses it: 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1. The correspondence is that a people's life comes from the Vinedresser's planting. The escalation is that fruit now comes by remaining in the Vine, John 15:4-5, so the failure of Israel is answered by a faithful Israel in one person. The type falls short because the old vine was a nation among nations, while the true vine reaches every believer from every nation.

typology.type: The Shepherd enthroned between the cherubim, Psalm 80:1
typology.fulfillment: The Shepherd is enthroned on the ark, in the holiest place. In Christ the throne and the shepherd meet. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and Revelation 7:17 says the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. The ark was seen only by the high priest once a year, while the Shepherd on the throne is now approached with confidence. The type falls short because the ark could be captured, as in 1 Samuel 4:11, whereas the throne of the Lamb cannot.

typology.type: The man at God's right hand, Psalm 80:17
typology.fulfillment: The psalm asks that God's hand be upon a man at His right hand. Psalm 110:1 gives the king that seat, and the apostles say it was given to Jesus. Peter preaches that God 'exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel,' Acts 5:31, and Stephen sees the Son of Man standing there, Acts 7:56. The escalation is that the right-hand man is not merely strengthened by God but shares His throne. The type falls short of any human king, because no Davidic ruler could himself give forgiveness.

The blessing of Numbers 6:25 becomes the people's cry, and the New Testament shows where the shining came. Paul says God made His light shine in our hearts 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. On the mountain the disciples saw His face shine like the sun, Matthew 17:2. The correspondence is direct: the prayer to see God's face lit with favor is answered by a Person. The type is not exhausted, since believers still wait to see Him fully.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ by the figure of the vine. Israel, the vine from Egypt, was meant to fill the land with fruit and did not. Isaiah 5:4 records the vinedresser's question, 'What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it?' Jesus takes up that history in the parable of the tenants, Matthew 21:33-41. There the owner sends servants, then finally his son, and the tenants kill the son. The parable is sharper than the psalm because it names the cost: the vine is not simply trampled by outsiders, but the son is killed by those who ought to have honored him. Then Jesus says, 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1, and He gives Himself as the place where the broken vine becomes fruitful. In Him the people are replanted, and the prayer 'Attend to this vine' is answered by the Vinedresser's own Son becoming the vine.

It leads to Christ by the son whom God raised up for Himself. The double phrase of verses 15 and 17 leaves open who this is, and the New Testament answers. Jesus is the Son whom the Father sent last, and the one 'raised up' in the fullest sense, since God raised Him from the dead and exalted Him, Acts 2:33-36. The right hand of the psalm becomes the right hand of Psalm 110:1, which Peter applies to Jesus at Pentecost. When the high priest asked Jesus whether He was the Christ, He answered by joining the two titles: the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven,' Mark 14:62. He takes the phrase of Psalm 80:17 and the vision of Daniel 7:13 as His own.

It leads to Christ by suffering and restoration. Hebrews 2:6-9 takes the 'son of man' language of Psalm 8 and says that we see Jesus, made lower than the angels and now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death. The Son of Man at God's right hand is also the One who was cut down. The psalm's vine is 'cut down and burned,' verse 16, and the man at God's hand has to be strengthened to bring the vine back. The gospel says that the Son went into the burning Himself, and rose.

It leads to Christ by the face. The refrain begs for God's face to shine so that they may be saved. Paul says that God has shone His light in our hearts 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. What the psalm could only ask for is a Person you can meet.

A caution: the psalm does not name the Messiah, and the difficulty of verse 15 warns against building too much on one line. The claim is not that the psalmist foresaw Jesus in detail, but that the shape of his prayer, a broken vine and a chosen man at God's right hand, is exactly the shape of what God did.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God with several names, and it lets each one do a job. He is Shepherd, and so bound to care for a flock that cannot care for itself. He is enthroned between the cherubim, and so holy and unreachable except by His own arrangement. He is the God of Hosts, the commander of heaven's armies, and so able to save with more than human strength. The refrain climbs to the covenant name because the people are asking not just for power but for faithfulness.

The psalm holds together two things that are hard to keep together. God is angry, verse 4, and God is still addressed as the one who can end the anger. The people do not treat the anger as a reason to stop praying. They treat it as a reason to pray harder, on the ground that the God who is angry is also the God who planted the vine. The psalm never says God is unjust. It says He has done what He has done, and it asks Him to do something new.

It shows a God who is sovereign over both growth and ruin. The vine flourished because He cleared the ground and drove out the nations, verses 8-9. It is trampled because He broke down the walls, verse 12. There is no rival power in the picture: the boar is real, but the question is put to God. That is a hard doctrine, and it is also a comforting one, for it means that the One who allowed the ruin is the only One who can reverse it.

It shows a God who cares for what He has made. 'Look down from heaven and see!' verse 14, is a plea to a God who has not stopped watching. The vine is called 'the root Your right hand has planted,' and the language is the language of ownership and affection.

It shows a God whose face is the source of life. The refrain's constant request for the shining of His face makes it plain that the saving of the people is not an event apart from His presence. To be saved is to be seen with favor by Him.

For worship, the psalm gives words to people who are not sure God is listening. It says to bring that doubt into prayer, to name Him by every title He has given, and to keep asking for the shining of His face until it comes.

crossReferences.note: The priestly blessing asks that the LORD cause His face to shine upon His people. Psalm 80 takes those words and prays them three times in a crisis, as if to say: this is what You promised to give us. The refrain turns a blessing into an appeal to a promise.

The song of the vineyard tells how a vine planted on fertile ground produced sour fruit and was left to be trampled. Psalm 80 sees the same field from the other side. Isaiah shows why the walls came down; the psalm begs the owner to return and tend the vine.

Jacob's blessing calls Joseph a fruitful vine and names God as the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel. Psalm 80 brings both images together, the Shepherd of Joseph in verse 1 and the vine in verse 8, which suggests the psalmist is drawing on the old blessing to remind God of it.

The ark of the LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim, was brought from Shiloh to the battlefield. Psalm 80:1 uses the same title for the Shepherd of Israel, and the reminder is that the God who allowed the ark's capture is still the enthroned Lord.

Rachel weeps for her children, and God says of Ephraim, 'Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me?' The passage shows that the northern tribes of Psalm 80, Rachel's descendants, remain dear to God, and that He promises to have compassion on them.

A royal lament with several of the same images. God has broken down the king's walls, and all who pass by plunder him. Together with Psalm 80:12, it shows that the language of broken walls could be used of the people or the king, since the two are bound together.

One like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting dominion. Psalm 80:17 asks for a man at God's right hand; Daniel shows the man arriving with the kingdom. Together they give Jesus' use of the title its depth.

'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' The right-hand seat of Psalm 80:17 is given here to the Lord of David. Peter uses this verse at Pentecost to show that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:34-36.

Jesus' parable of the vineyard tenants echoes Isaiah 5 and the vine of Psalm 80. The owner's son is sent last and killed, and the vineyard is given to others who will produce fruit. It shows how the broken vine becomes the Son's rejection, and the Son's rejection becomes the cornerstone.

'I am the true vine.' Jesus places His people in Himself, where fruit is a matter of remaining. It answers the plea 'Attend to this vine' by making the vine a person, and it reverses the sad ending of verse 16 with the promise of fruit that lasts.

Asked whether He is the Christ, Jesus answers that the Son of Man will be seen 'sitting at the right hand of Power.' He joins the man at God's right hand with the Danielic Son of Man and claims both for Himself.

The face of God that the refrain begged to see shining appears in Christ. Paul says God's light shines in our hearts to give the knowledge of His glory 'in the face of Jesus Christ.' What the people asked for is now found in a person.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 80 stands in the middle of a very long story of a vine. In Genesis 49 Joseph is a fruitful vine and God is his Shepherd. In Exodus 15 God plants His people on His mountain. In the psalm the vine has been planted, has grown to the borders of the land, and has been broken. In Isaiah 5 the owner, tired of sour fruit, pulls down the wall. In Ezekiel 19 the vine is uprooted and burned, and in Hosea 10:1 the more fruit it had, the more altars it built. The whole story is one of a people who are planted with care and do not bear what the Gardener wanted.

The psalm captures the moment when the people can no longer help themselves. They cannot repair the walls or restore the fruit. They can only ask God to turn, and so the question of the whole Old Testament is put in its purest form: who can restore the vine when the vine cannot restore itself? The psalm's answer is a man at God's right hand, a son whom God has strengthened, and its plea is that God's hand be on him.

The story does not answer at once. The northern kingdom falls; Judah is later cast out too. But the prophets keep the hope alive. Isaiah 27:2-6 sings again of a fruitful vineyard in which the LORD says He is not angry, and promises that Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit. Jeremiah 31 says God will bring Ephraim home. Daniel sees the Son of Man given a kingdom that will not be destroyed.

The New Testament brings those lines together in Jesus. He is the last Son sent to the vineyard, killed and raised, the true vine in whom the people are replanted, and the Son of Man at God's right hand. The face that shone in the priestly blessing shines in Him, 2 Corinthians 4:6. The church now lives as the branches, John 15:5, called to bear fruit by remaining in Him.

The end of the story finishes what the refrain asks. In the new creation there is no more curse and no more night, and God's servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:3-5. The prayer 'cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved' becomes a fact, and the vine, at last, fills the earth.

quiz.q: How does the psalm address God in its opening verses, 1-2?

options.text: As the Shepherd of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, who leads His people like a flock.
options.note: Verse 1 opens with exactly this shepherd and enthroned imagery.

options.text: As a distant, uninvolved observer of Israel's troubles.
options.note: The psalm addresses God as intimately involved, not distant.

options.text: As a warrior with no relationship to Israel's tribes.
options.note: God's mighty power is invoked, verse 2, but within a shepherd-and-people relationship, not detachment.

options.text: As one of several gods Israel worshiped.
options.note: The psalm addresses the one true God exclusively, not one among several.

quiz.q: What has happened to the vine God brought out of Egypt, verses 12-13?

options.text: Its walls have been broken down, so that passersby pick its fruit and wild boars ravage it.
options.note: Verses 12-13 describe exactly this devastation.

options.text: It has grown to cover the whole earth without any trouble.
options.note: The psalm describes the vine's earlier flourishing, verses 9-11, but now its present ruin.

options.text: It was never planted at all.
options.note: Verses 8-11 describe God planting and establishing the vine.

options.text: It has been carefully replanted in a safer location.
options.note: The text describes destruction and vulnerability, not relocation.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God to place His hand upon, in verse 17?

options.text: The man at God's right hand, the son of man He has raised up for Himself.
options.note: Verse 17 makes this specific request.

options.text: A newly built temple.
options.note: No temple building is mentioned in this request.

options.text: The armies of the surrounding nations.
options.note: The request concerns a specific man at God's right hand, not foreign armies.

options.text: The boundaries of the land itself.
options.note: The request is personal, about a man at God's right hand, not territorial boundaries.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's repeated refrain, appearing in verses 3, 7, and 19?

options.text: "Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved."
options.note: This exact refrain repeats three times with intensifying divine titles.

options.text: "We will never call on Your name again."
options.note: The refrain is a plea for restoration, not a rejection of God.

options.text: "Our own strength will save us."
options.note: The refrain credits God alone with the power to save, not human strength.

options.text: "The nations will never trouble us again."
options.note: The refrain is directed to God's restoring action, not a claim about future peace from enemies.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's imagery connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Jesus calls Himself the true vine, and He is the Son of Man exalted to God's right hand, fulfilling both central images.
options.note: John 15:1 and Daniel 7:13 with Acts 5:31 supply these direct connections.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament at all.
options.note: The vine and son of man imagery are picked up directly by Jesus and the apostles.

options.text: It only refers to a literal, historical vineyard with no further meaning.
options.note: The psalm uses the vine as a metaphor for Israel, which the New Testament develops further in Christ.

options.text: It predicts the precise date of Jerusalem's rebuilding.
options.note: The psalm's imagery concerns restoration and a coming figure, not a rebuilding timeline.

questions: The psalm pictures Israel as a vine God Himself planted and once caused to flourish, verses 8-11. Where in your life has God clearly done the planting and growing, and where do you need to trust Him with the ravaged places?
The refrain 'restore us, cause Your face to shine' repeats and intensifies through the psalm. What situation are you tempted to give up praying about, when this psalm calls you to keep pleading?

The psalm names real anger and real tears, 'the bread of tears,' verse 5, without pretending everything is fine. Where do you need to bring honest lament to God rather than a performance of composure?
The psalm's hope finally rests on 'the son of man' at God's right hand, verse 17, fulfilled in Jesus. How does knowing Christ already holds that place change how you pray for restoration today?

The people promise, 'we will not turn away from You... we will call on Your name,' verse 18, once revived. What would renewed devotion to God look like for you this week, in light of what He has already done in Christ?

translationNotes.note: 'Shepherd of Israel' and 'enthroned between the cherubim' both recall the ark of the covenant, where God's presence was pictured as dwelling among His people.
'The Sea' refers to the Mediterranean, and 'the River' to the Euphrates, marking the fullest extent of the land promise, Genesis 15:18, that the flourishing vine once filled.

'The son of man' (ben adam) simply means a human being in ordinary Hebrew usage, yet its placement at God's right hand gave later readers, including Daniel 7:13 and the Gospels, grounds to hear a messianic hope here.
